The wrong diagnosis is usually "people were lazy." If nobody stuck to the hierarchy, the taxonomy probably asked for decisions people couldn't make confidently or quickly, so they dumped files wherever was fastest. Before redesigning, look at where things actually landed last term: the junk pile is the map of what the structure didn't cover.

Concretely, what I'd change:

Keep the hierarchy shallow, two or three levels at most. Deep nesting means each file needs four correct choices to get placed, and people take the shortcut.

Organize by project, not by type. A folder per project with its own loose contents beats a drive-wide Documents/Data/Analysis tree, because a file's project is usually obvious and its type often isn't. If you keep any type folders, restrict them to shared evergreen things.

Name folders after language people already use in conversation, not formal categories. The test is whether someone can guess where a file goes without asking.

For stale junk: don't rely on a cleanup day. Either set retention rules (archives folder, anything untouched in X months moves, with a calendar rule or a script) or make deletion somebody's actual job with a recurring slot. Junk that "nobody" owns never gets cleared. A monthly 20-minute sweep with one named owner beats a policy nobody enforces.

Then the part that decides whether any of this survives: name it in one place, and model it. Put the one-page map where people see it, put new files there yourself for a few weeks, and fix misplacements quietly rather than announcing a new system. Enforcement through habit change sticks; enforcement through a memo doesn't.

The design also has to fit your group's actual size. How many people, and what kind of files dominate, datasets, code, or papers and drafts?
